comparator.name: Film and Literary Studies
comparator.sourceNotes: The current official 2026-2027 prospectus API reconstructs a complete 180-EC curriculum. The 60-EC first year and 25-EC second-year common core are compulsory. The normalized generic target does not name a specialisation; the Film Studies track is selected by the documented official-order tie break. Its 35-EC second-year track is compulsory. For the 20-EC third-year Film Studies option group, Film and Philosophy (10 EC), Third Cinema (5 EC), and Cinema & the Digital (5 EC) form a valid complete selection. The 10-EC bachelor thesis and 30 EC of genuine elective space complete the degree. No optional course was selected for UCR convenience.

comparatorRouteSelection.basis: The normalized target is generic and Leiden publishes equally general Film Studies and Literary Studies tracks after the shared first-year and common second-year core. alternativeSelection.assessment: The broad closest match owns the direct film-and-literature, close-reading, narrative, historical and theoretical interests. Two further generator-backed directions are coherent, feasible and materially distinct: a global and transmedial storytelling route, and a culture, identity and social-debate route. Their schedules differ pairwise by seven to fourteen courses and all satisfy the hard constraints, so the maximum of three alternatives is reached.

comparisonAlignment.rationale: Both introduce analysis of visual representation and signifying practices in historical cultural context.
Both examine representation, identity and difference across cultural and postcolonial contexts.
Both introduce literary analysis and theory through close reading and critical interpretation.
Both introduce film forms, histories and genre-based analytical concepts.
Both study literary works across historical periods and movements; UCR is comparative rather than movement-specific.
Both analyse how verbal and visual form produce meaning; UCR concentrates on rhetoric and style.
Both examine changing media technologies, histories and digital or material forms.
Both compare narrative and literary traditions across cultures and periods.
Both examine documentary form, audiovisual evidence, representation and creative non-fiction practice.
Both analyse race, representation and power in screen media; UCR is broader than the Third Cinema tradition.
Both study relations between literary texts and film, including adaptation and medium-specific meaning.
Both examine literary meaning, interpretation and non-dominant forms; UCR lacks the dedicated poetry-and-cinema pairing.
Both critically analyse contemporary audiovisual media and technology; UCR focuses on environmental media.
Both analyse films, texts and media in relation to current public and social concerns.
Both develop philosophical reasoning about value and contested judgments; UCR is not specifically philosophy of film.
Both provide philosophical foundations for questions of knowledge and method; UCR is broader than philosophy of science.
Both place cultural forms in historical movements; UCR is broad modern history rather than cinema-specific.
Both develop qualitative research, interpretation, academic writing and presentation; UCR is not limited to film and literature.
Both require sustained independent humanities research and a substantial evidence-based academic argument; UCR is a course rather than a compulsory thesis.

notes.text: Leiden requires an integrated sequence in film and literary theory, close text-image analysis, named cinematic and literary movements, world cinema and literature, adaptation and intermediality, documentary, digital cinema, a 10-EC thesis and other specialist film courses. UCR can assemble strong combinations in literature, film and media, art history, communication, philosophy, cultural history and research, but it lacks this dedicated compulsory film-and-literature sequence and has no compulsory bachelor thesis; the standardised Optional independent research element remains optional.
